author: Shimada
asr_identification: Dharanikota (Dharanikoṭa), right bank of the Krishna, Guntur district, Andhra Pradesh
evidence: Fortified city adjacent to the Amaravati stupa: roughly square, mud fortifications c. 600 m a side, moat-cum-wharf (IAR 1962-63); radiocarbon dates for the founding of the fortifications c. 475±100 to 205±100 BCE; NBPW at Dharanikota, Amaravati and Vaddamanu; wharfs of wood then brick, with Palnad limestone pieces (Raghavachary).
quote: evidence in this regard is the establishment of Dhaṃñakaṭaka (present Dharanikoṭa), the fortified city adjacent to the stūpa (Map 3). As the contours of the present township still show, the ancient city was roughly square in shape and was surrounded by mud fortifications (ca. 600 metres on each side).
note: Agrees with the study's Dharanikota capital (10.14, medium) and Mizutani; adds the radiocarbon date of the rampart but, like the IAR reports, nothing for the 7th century. The c. 2.4 km circuit is far short of the Xiyu ji's 40 li for the capital, a mismatch the note could record; does not change medium.

author: Shimada
asr_identification: Amaravati great stupa, less than 1 km E of the E wall of Dharanikota
evidence: Stupa and city separated only by the fortifications and a reservoir, the stupa under 1 km from the city's eastern wall, on a plain, not a hill; Amaravati inscriptions record donations from the Dhaṃñakaṭaka nigama, so the two are 'a unit' (Begley).
quote: since it was located close to Dharanikoṭa, the ancient fortified city Dhaṃñakaṭaka (Map 8). Although the two sites are divided by fortifications and a reservoir, the distance between the stūpa and the eastern wall of the city is less than one kilometre. Unlike Sānchī, the stūpa is not built on a hill, but on a plain.
note: Agrees with the study's layout (great stupa just E of the Dharanikota city = eastern convent, 10.14.02a, medium) on bearing and distance. But Shimada stresses that the stupa stands on a plain, while the Xiyu ji puts Pūrvaśaila 城東據山 'resting on a mountain' E of the city; this tells against Amaravati = Pūrvaśaila in detail. Shimada does not name the convent.

author: Shimada
asr_identification: Pūrvaśaila monasteries at Allūru and Takkellapādu (Krishna district); Aparaśaila at Ghaṇṭasāla; Amaravati stupa held by the Caityakas
evidence: Inscriptions of the 1st-2nd c. CE assign sites to sects: the Amaravati stupa to the Caityakas; Ghaṇṭasāla to the Aparaśailas; Allūru and Takkellapādu to the Pūrvaśailas; Kesānapalli to the Bahuśrutīyas. In the site table, pillar inscriptions from one excavated monastery name the Puvaseliya (Pūrvaśaila) sect.
quote: An Amarāvatī inscription records that the stūpa was in the possession of the Caityakas around the 1-2nd century ce.65 Similarly, Ghaṇṭasāla belonged to the Aparaśailas; Allūru and Takkellapādu passed to the Pūrvaśailas
note: Differs in detail from the study's Amaravati = Pūrvaśaila (10.14.02a): the epigraphic Pūrvaśailas are at Allūru and Takkellapādu across the river, the Amaravati stupa itself was Caityaka, and Aparaśailas sat at coastal Ghaṇṭasāla, not W of the capital. Sect names are of schools, 500 years before Xuanzang, so they do not locate his two convents; with Puvasela at Nāgārjunakoṇḍa this confirms that the names were not unique. Leaves 10.14.02a medium as inferred from position only, 10.14.02b open.

author: Shimada
asr_identification: war camp at Dhāṃñakaṭaka; Aparaseliya monastery at Pithunda, unidentified, N of Dhāṃñakaṭaka
evidence: Pātagaṇḍigūḍem copper plate (West Godavari), the oldest copper-plate grant in India: the Ikṣvāku Ehuvula Cāṃtamūla (c. 263-283 to 287-307 CE), in 'the victorious war camp at Dhāṃñakaṭaka', granted land to Aparaseliya monks at Pithunda to repair their monastery.
quote: in ‘the victorious war camp at Dhāṃñakaṭaka’ made a land grant to Aparaseliya monks in Pithunda (an unidentified place in the north of Dhāṃñakaṭaka) to repair their monastery.
note: Adds a 3rd-c. Aparaśaila monastery in Dhānyakaṭaka's neighbourhood, but Pithunda is unlocated and Shimada puts it N, not W, of the city; it does not locate Xuanzang's Avaraśaila (10.14.02b, open, low). Agrees with the study that Dhānyakaṭaka was a royal seat; nothing on the 7th c.

author: Shimada
asr_identification: Amaravati and the lower Krishna valley
evidence: No major construction at Amaravati after c. 250 CE; late pieces small and carved on the backs of earlier slabs; textual and epigraphic evidence shows many Buddhist sites incl. Amaravati known mainly as Śaiva sites in the 7th-11th c., Śiva temples reusing limestone from monasteries. Cites Xuanzang (via Beal II p. 221) for numerous but mostly ruined monasteries, about 20 surviving, about 100 Deva temples.
quote: Textual and epigraphic evidence shows that many Buddhist sites, including Amarāvatī, became known primarily as Śaivite sites in the 7-11th century.5 … reported that monasteries at Dhanakaṭaka were numerous but were mostly ruined. Surviving monasteries were about twenty, while there were about a hundred Hindu (Deva) shrines.
note: Agrees with the Dharanikota/Amaravati identification and fits the Xiyu ji's ruined monasteries and the two convents empty for over a century (10.14.02a); the decline after 250 CE adds archaeological context but no site evidence for the 7th-c. capital. Medium stands.

author: Shimada
evidence: Peddavegi identified as Vengipura of the Śālaṅkāyanas; Sarma's excavation found a stupa inside the fortification near the northern wall.
quote: At Peddavegi, identified as ancient Vengipura of the Śālaṅkāyana dynasty, a stūpa was discovered inside the fortification near the northern wall.
note: Agrees with the study's capital Veṅgī at Peddavegi (10.13, high); repeats Sarma 2002, no new evidence.

author: Ambekar et al.
evidence: Name on the site: two sealings with the legend 'Anandpur rajño' from the Kshatrapa level of the Vadnagar excavation; Kumārapāla's inscription of 1152 CE at the Arjunbari gate naming Anandpur; Maitraka copper plates naming Anandpur, Nagar, Anartapur; epigraphic record 600-1300 CE.
quote: the Solanki king Kumarpal’s inscription of 1152 CE at Arjunbari gates also mentions the name Anandpur designating Vadnagar … The name of Anandpur can be further stretched back to 400 years i.e. to the early-Kshatrapa phase based on the two sealings bearing the legend Anandpur rajño unearthed from the Kshatrapa level deposit of Vadnagar excavation.
note: Agrees with the study's Vadnagar (11.09, high) and Mizutani; new site evidence: excavated sealings naming Ānandapura carry the name on the spot back to the Kshatrapa period, closing the gap the note admits (praśasti only 12th-century). Does not address the Life's route figures, which fit near Ahmadabad better.

author: Ambekar et al.
evidence: Gujarat State excavation 2006-12: monastery inside the fortified area at Ghaskol (courtyard with cells, votive stupas, Buddha head, plaque of the monkey's gift of honey, inscribed Brahmi bowls); circular brick stupa at Ambaghat on Sharmishtha lake in Period III (1st-4th c. CE) with 34 sealings 'namassarvajñāya' (as on a Devnimori casket); elliptical shrine with stupas outside the fort; Buddhist cave dwellings at Taranga 30 km N, Buddhism there to the 14th c. The excavators date the monasteries to the 1st c. CE.
quote: In fact, the finding of a Bodhisattva image in 1992 provided the first concrete evidence for Vadnagar’s association with Buddhism … The most significant discovery at the site is a Buddhist monastery which is located within the fortified area consisting of an open courtyard in the centre surrounded by cells on all four sides.
note: Agrees (11.09): a monastic town as the Xiyu ji's 'some ten saṃghārāmas' requires, though the excavated Buddhist levels are dated early centuries CE, not shown in use in the 7th c.

author: Ambekar et al.
evidence: ASI Excavation Branch V, eight seasons 2014-22: c. 24 m of deposit, seven cultural periods, continuous occupation from mid-8th c. BCE to the present; earthen rampart of the 2nd c. BCE later rebuilt in brick and stone on the same line; never abandoned.
quote: Reaffirmation of the identification of Anandpur (as Vadnagar) found mentioned in the copper plate grants (Maitraka of Vallabhi), travel records of Xuan Zhuang, inscriptions with reference to Vadnagar and through subsequent excavation have been successful.
note: Agrees (11.09, high): the excavation shows a walled town occupied through Xuanzang's time, as his capital of 20 li requires.

author: Patnaik
asr_identification: Radhanagar (Kankia), Dharmasala area, Jajpur district, Odisha
evidence: Excavation 2010-13 of a fortified city with bastions, gateways and moat; AMS date 412-354 cal BCE (Beta 627793); urban occupation from the 4th c. BCE to the 3rd-4th c. CE; Brahmi inscription 'Sadabhu Tissa'; Buddhist finds. Sisupalgarh's urban phase begins only after the 2nd c. BCE and yields no Buddhist antiquities, so Patnaik reassigns Sisupalgarh to Khāravela's Kaliṅganagarī and Tosali to Radhanagar.
quote: Previously, Toshali, the provincial headquarters of Ashoka and a significant urban center in the 3rd century BCE, was identified with Sisupalgarh-Dhauli (Sahu, 1964; Brandtner, 1988-89). However, recent excavations at Radhanagar have provided new insights, challenging this identification … likely corresponding to Toshali Nagar, the provincial headquarters of Emperor Ashoka
note: Bears on the Oḍra capital (10.09, open, Jajpur most often): if Tosali is Radhanagar in Jajpur district, 高桑's/Ji's Dhauli = Tosalī argument no longer points S of the Mahānadī but to the Jajpur area, near the study's leading candidate. Radhanagar's urban phase ends in the 3rd-4th c. CE, so it is not site evidence for a 7th-c. capital; no mention of Xuanzang. The capital stays open.

author: Patnaik
asr_identification: Radhanagar (some scholars); Dantapuram fort, right bank of the Vamsadhara, Srikakulam district
evidence: Reports the identification of Radhanagar with the Dantapura of Pali literature (Prusti, Mohanty & Mishra 2000) as one view; compares Radhanagar's fortification with the planned fort at Dantapuram on the Vamsadhara, Srikakulam district.
quote: A comparable fortification is observed at the Dantapuram site (now in Srikakulam District, Andhra Pradesh) on the right bank of the Vamsadhara River. … Some scholars identify this settlement with the earliest city of Dantapura mentioned in Pali literature (Prusti, Mohanty & Mishra, 2000), while others associate it with Toshali Nagar.
note: Concerns the early historic Kaliṅga capital of the tooth-relic legend, not Xuanzang's 7th-c. capital (10.11, open: Kalingapatnam or Mukhalingam); Patnaik himself prefers Tosali for Radhanagar. The Dantapuram fort on the Vaṃśadhārā lies in the same Srikakulam area as the study's two candidates. No change.

author: Patnaik
asr_identification: Langudi and Kayama hills, Jajpur district
evidence: Langudi and Kayama: brick stupas and monastic remains, caves, a 3 m elephant sculpture, a 4th-5th c. shell-script inscription, and at Langudi an inscribed bust read 'Chhikarena ranj Ashokena' (B.N. Mukherjee); dated 3rd c. BCE to 6th c. CE.
quote: The sites of Langudi and Kayma (Figure 3) have yielded antiquities and structural remains from the early historic period, dating from the 3rd century BCE to the 6th century CE.
note: Does not mention Puṣpagiri or Xuanzang; the Langudi = Puṣpagiri claim (bibliography) is not made here. Background only for 10.09.02 (study: Khandagiri/Udayagiri).

author: Besenval
asr_identification: no site: Kech-Makran (Pakistani Makran), period VII not found
evidence: French mission survey and soundings (Miri Qalat near Turbat, Kech, Nihing and Dasht valleys, the coast to Gwadar/Jiwani): eight-period sequence; period VII ('indo-sassanide', 6th/7th c.) is assigned to the Buddhist population reported by Xuanzang and Indian texts (with alternating Persian and Indian rule, after Wink 1990), but it has not yet been identified in the recorded remains; early Islamic sites are of the 10th-12th c. The Iranian coast was not surveyed.
quote: La période VII (période indo-sassanide, rae/viie s. ap. J.-C.) Cette période correspondrait à l'important peuplement bouddhiste signalé par le pèlerin chinois Hiuen Tsang et les textes indiens pour le début du vne siècle.
note: Agrees with the study that the capital of Laṅgala is unlocated (11.19, open, low). Adds negative survey evidence for the Kech valley (Turbat), on the Las Bela-Persian Makran road, as Stein had found; says nothing of Lākoriān or of Persian Makran (Kasarkand), which it did not survey. No bearing on Pārsa (11.20).
